column1: Project lifecycle: Create a project scoped to an organisation
column26:
Related to user story B1

Projects hold related work — the client's example is an "Autonomous Driving"
project carrying several annotation and evaluation tasks. The capability
largely exists; what is missing is the organisation scoping and the proof of it.

h1. I can create a project and see it listed in my organisation.

h1. A project belongs to exactly one organisation and is visible only to that organisation's members.

h1. I can open a project and see the tasks inside it.

Scope note worth putting on the ticket: this is hardening, not net-new. The work is confirming POST /organizations/{org_id}/projects scopes to the caller's org, a test that a project in org A is invisible to org B, and making project-create-form.tsx surface real validation errors. Pairs with SCRUM-45, which does update/archive on the same object.

column1: Organisation Management: Invite, remove and role-manage members
column26:
Related to user story J3

You cannot run governed review without the people who perform it. This is the
administrator-facing capability on top of the invitation flow.

h1. I can invite a person, see pending invitations, and remove a member.

h1. I can assign and change a member's role.

h1. A role change takes effect on what that person can actually do.

Issues 17, 18
Blocked by SCRUM-8 until the invitation flow works.

column1: Project: Overview of status and progress
column26:
Related to user story J2

A starting point, not an analytics product.

h1. Shows project status, item counts by state and basic workflow statistics.

h1. Figures agree with the task and export screens.

h1. Deliberately limited — the client asked that time not be spent making this comprehensive.

The one that will actually take effort is criterion 2: the figures have to reconcile with SCRUM-43 (B6/H5, aligning task completion and export readiness). Don't start this before SCRUM-43 settles the counting rule, or you'll implement it twice.

column1: Organisation Management: Stable organisation identifier and URL
column26:
Related to user story J1

The client's one concrete requirement in this area is being able to refer to an
organisation unambiguously.

h1. Each organisation has a unique identifier and URL that do not change.

h1. An organisation can hold multiple accounts and use cases.

Keep it small — the backlog explicitly says so.

column1: Annotation: Configurable AI suggestion visibility
column26:
Related to user story C4

Seeing the machine's answer first changes the answer people give. The code has
two modes; the client brief requires three.

h1. I can select human-only, AI-first, or blind-then-reveal when setting up a task.

h1. In blind-then-reveal the reviewer cannot see the AI suggestion until their own answer is recorded.

h1. The mode in force is recorded against the item, so results from different modes can be compared later.

Test that the suggestion is absent from the API response before the human commits, not merely hidden in the UI. SCRUM-73 (I4, "measure what AI assistance does to human judgement") cannot produce a result unless this records the mode — worth linking them.

column1: Review: Prevent self-review of own annotations
column26:
Related to user story D1

review_actions.py:206 checks organisation membership only, so an annotator can
approve their own work. A review one person can perform on their own output is
not a review, and any dataset built on it is indefensible.

h1. Attempting to review my own annotation is refused, with an explanation rather than a bare 403.

h1. Only users holding a reviewer or expert role can perform review actions at all.

h1. The same restriction applies to dispute decisions, not only first-line review.

Issue 7

column1: Task lifecycle: Create annotation and judgement tasks with a result shape
column26:
Related to user story B3

The client's two task categories need different work surfaces and different
result shapes. Task creation exists; the annotation-versus-judgement
distinction and the result shape do not.



I can create a task under a project, choosing annotation or judgement and the task type.



The task records what a finished result should look like — labels for annotation, verdict plus reasoning for judgement.



Text tasks work end to end; image and video tasks can be created without breaking, but are not committed demo paths this phase.



The real work here is label_schema_ref: today it's a string pointer nothing reads, and it has to resolve to an actual result shape. Borrow the MVP's SchemaMerger idea but map fields explicitly rather than asking a model to infer them. Blocks SCRUM-24 (B4, lifecycle transitions) from being meaningful.

column1: Schema: Replace hardcoded credentials
column26:
A4

# No live credential is readable in the source code.
# Credentials are supplied per environment and can be rotated without a code change.
# The exposed key is rotated at the provider, not merely removed from the code.

*Issue 1* (live API key hardcoded in committed source) — this story's first criterion removes it, and the rotation criterion covers the part a code fix alone can't: the key is already public in every existing clone. Depends on *A3*, since configuration must actually load before a key can be supplied any other way.

column1: Trustworthy Foundations
Schema: Restore existing testcases
column26:
A2

# The web application's checks and test suite pass cleanly, so a broken change is caught before merge rather than after.
# Tests that claim to check something actually check it — a test named for image-annotation loading must fail if that loading breaks.
# Test setup does not imply behaviour the platform doesn't have

*Issues 12 & 13* (frontend fails typecheck; test suite failing) — this story's definition of done is a green frontend build and suite, so both are resolved by the work itself rather than tracked separately.
*Issue 25* (a frontend test passes even when the behaviour it names is broken) — replacing the placeholder assertion with a real one is exactly what “tests genuinely pass” requires here.
*Issue 26* (misleading mock setup in a backend test) — removed while making the suite trustworthy, so a future reader isn't misled about what the code does.

column1: Schema: Fix db setup issues
column26:
A3

# Following the documented setup steps produces a running platform with the seeded Admin, Reviewer and Annotator accounts.
# Resetting the demo data works repeatedly, including against an already-seeded database.
# Configuration supplied by a team member (ports, keys, environment) is actually picked up by the platform.
# A setup failure reports what went wrong instead of failing silently or crashing while reporting.

*Issue 24* (init_data.py --reset broken two ways) — the story requires reset to work repeatedly on a stock Windows terminal, which closes both the console-encoding crash and the foreign-key failure that currently leaves the database half-dropped.
*Issue 23* (.env config silently ignored) — “configuration is actually picked up” is the acceptance criterion, so the wrong-prefix and never-read-the-file defects both have to go for this story to pass.

column1: Evaluation Harness and Casebook
Evaluation8: Findings record including negative results
column26:
Negative findings tell the client more about the platform's real limits than a list of features that worked, and the brief states plainly that they carry equal weight. Depends on EV2, EV4.

*Subtasks*

# Record the findings, including what failed and why — negative results reported rather than dropped.
# Trace each finding to a specific case so a reader can re-run it.
# Report negative results rather than filtering them out.
# Feed the technical report and the what-did-not-work record from this.

Story *I5* — I can prove the platform's records hold up
Issues none

column1: Evaluation7: Integrity checks on provenance, roles and releases
column26:
Integrity claimed is not integrity demonstrated. These are the checks that let someone outside the team verify a release rather than take it on trust. Depends on EV2, F1, H2.

*Subtasks*

# Check that every released item has complete provenance.
# Check that governed actions were performed by users holding the right role.
# Reconstruct a release from its manifest and compare it against the original.
# Fail the check loudly rather than warning, so an integrity gap cannot pass unnoticed.

Story *I5* — I can prove the platform's records hold up
Issues none

column1: Evaluation6: Measure what AI assistance does to human judgement
column26:
The client's actual question — not whether assistance feels faster, but what it does to the answers people give. Impossible while the suggestion and the decision are collapsed into one value. Depends on EV2, F3, C4.

*Subtasks*

# Report accept, modify and override rates per task.
# Report time per item alongside them.
# Compare results across the execution modes from C4.
# Report how often a confidently wrong suggestion was accepted.
# Impossible unless suggestion and decision stay separate — depends on F3.

Story *I4* — I can see what AI assistance does to human judgement
Issues none

column1: Evaluation5: Reviewer agreement and AI suggestion quality
column26:
Raw percentage match flatters any task where one answer dominates. Report a real coefficient, and report whether the assistant's stated confidence tracks whether it was actually right. Depends on EV2, D7.

*Subtasks*

# Report agreement with an established coefficient rather than raw percentage match.
# Report per task and comparably across tasks.
# Report AI suggestion quality and confidence calibration alongside human agreement.
# Measure against the gold annotations in the fixture sets.
# Depends on D7's cross-validation routing.

Story *I3* — I can tell whether reviewers actually agree
Issues none

column1: Evaluation4: Grow the casebook to 40–60 cases
column26:
A standing commitment from the week it lands, not a block of work at the end. Assembling the casebook in the final fortnight is the failure the brief warns about by name. Depends on EV3.

*Subtasks*

# Grow toward the 40–60 cases the brief specifies, each ticket contributing the cases for its own surface as it lands.
# Map each workflow surface to the cases it owes.
# Add “lands its own cases” to the definition of done for every feature ticket.
# Backfill cases for the surfaces already built.
# Review the count against the 40–60 target at the weekly meeting.

Story *I2* — The platform is tested against cases designed to break it
Issues none

column1: Evaluation3: Casebook structure and the adversarial categories
column26:
The seven categories the brief names, written as real cases against the gold fixture datasets. A system demonstrated on easy items proves nothing about the ones that matter. Depends on EV1.

*Subtasks*

# Write the adversarial categories the brief names, starting with a confidently wrong AI suggestion.
# Cover a genuinely ambiguous item, and reviewers who disagree with no guideline resolution.
# Cover a guideline changed after annotation, and an item with missing provenance.
# Cover an unreviewed item reaching a proposed release, and a release containing a superseded item.
# Use the gold fixtures in labeling_ai_assistnat_mvp/app/data/text/ — four 200-item sets with ground truth, already shaped in hej's own vocabulary.
# Define the case template — inputs, steps, expected outcome, category.

Story *I2* — The platform is tested against cases designed to break it
Issues none

column1: Evaluation2: Repeatable runs and regression reporting
column26:
A run that cannot be repeated proves nothing, and a result nobody can compare hides regressions rather than revealing them. Depends on EV1, A3.

*Subtasks*

# Keep results comparable across runs so a regression is visible.
# Reset to a clean seeded database between runs — depends on A3.
# Script the mock assistant's responses so a scenario has one correct outcome.
# Emit a machine-readable result per case alongside the human summary.
# Give each case a stable id and diff a run against the previous one.

Story *I1* — I can re-run the whole workflow against known cases
Issues none

column1: Evaluation1: Scenario harness that drives the workflow end to end
column26:
Testing individual pieces says nothing about whether the workflow holds together. This is the runner and the step vocabulary it executes — project, policy, task, items, AI pass, annotate, review, dispute, adjudicate, release.

*Subtasks*

# Build a harness that drives a scenario end to end without manual clicking.
# Cover annotation, review, cross-validation, dispute and final judgement in a single run.
# State the expected outcome per scenario and report pass or fail.
# Define the scenario file format — named steps plus the outcome each one expects.
# Have steps act as distinct seeded users, so role separation is exercised rather than bypassed.
# Prove the loop with one trivial scenario before any real cases are written.

Story *I1* — I can re-run the whole workflow against known cases
Issues none
